President Trump three times used the FVRA in unprecedented ways 
to expand his potential influence over agencies. The first matter involved 
the Consumer Finance Protection Bureau. As explained in Chapter 2, the 
CFPB is outside the ordinary appropriations process, along with the 
oversight that process entails, because the Dodd-Frank Act provides for the 
Bureau to be funded out of the budget aUocated to the Federal Reserve 
System 12 U.S.C. § 5497(a)(l)-(2).) It is also unusual among independent 
agencies because it is administered by only a single head. Republican 
Senators used the filibuster to forestall President Obama’s nomination oi 
Richard Cordray to be the CFPB’s inaugural director, often arguing that 
the Dodd-Frank Act, which created the CFPB, had unwisely vested 
extraordinary institutional independence in an agency headed by only a 
single administrator. At the same time President Obama made the recess 
appointments challenged in Noel Canning, he also gave a recess 
appointment to Cordray; following the decision in Noel Canning and the 
change in Senate rules eliminating fihbusters for executive branch 
appointments, the Senate confirmed Cordray to a full seven-year term, 
which would have terminated in the summer of 2018. The position became 
vacant in November 2017, however, because Cordray resigned to make 
what turned out to be an unsuccessful race for the Ohio governorship.
As with many agencies. Congress, in creating the CFPB, provided by 
statute for how a vacancy in the directorship would be handled. Under ^12 
U.S.C. § 5491(b)(5)(B), the Deputy Director is to become acting director “in 
the absence or unavailability of the Director.” Yet OLC had previously held 
that the FVRA provisions for presidential appointments in cases of vacancy 
were still available as an option for the President, even in the face of agency 
statutes setting forth specific orders of succession. General A.uth, of the 
President to Name an Acting Attorney Gen,, 2007 WL 5334854 (O.L.C. Sept. 
17, 2007)—a position affirmed in a different matter by the Ninth Circuit. 
Hooks V. Kitsap Tenant Support Services, 816 F.3d 550, 555—56 (9th Cir. 
2016). Under 5 U.S.C. § 3345, the President “may direct a person who 
serves in an office for which appointment is required to be made by the 
President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to perform the 
functions and duties of the vacant office temporarily in an acting capacity. 
For the first timp. ever. President Trump used this authority not to appoint 
a different •individual from within the agency to become acting head, but 
rather to appoint as Acting Director the Senate-confirmed head of a 
different agency—specifically, 0MB Director Mick Mulvaney. After a 
District Court denied Deputy Director Leandra English a preliminary 
injunction to prevent the takeover, she dropped her suit. English v. Trump, 
279 F. Supp. 3d 307 (D.D.C.), appeal dismissed. No. 18—5007 (D.C. Cir. July 
13, 2018).
President Trump made a second unusual FVRA appointment after his
